n: This chapter is written as a royal proclamation from Nebuchadnezzar himself to the whole world—a pagan king’s personal testimony of how God humbled him.

f.w: Peace be multiplied unto you
f.g: A standard greeting in royal letters.

n: The king wants everyone to know the miraculous signs the Most High God has done for him.

f.w: the high God

n: His praise opens and closes the chapter: God’s kingdom is everlasting. The proud emperor who thought his own kingdom was golden now confesses God’s greater kingdom.

f.w: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom

n: The story begins at the height of Nebuchadnezzar’s comfort and success—relaxed and prosperous in his palace.

f.w: flourishing
f.g: Literally “green” like a thriving tree—anticipating the dream.

n: A dream frightens him and disturbs his thoughts.
He calls in all Babylon’s wise men to explain it.
Once again, Babylon’s experts fail—though this time the king tells them the dream.
Finally Daniel comes. The king describes him as having “the spirit of the holy gods”—a pagan way of recognizing God’s Spirit in Daniel.

f.w: the spirit of the holy gods
according to the name of my god
f.g: Belteshazzar contains the name of Bel (Marduk), Babylon’s chief god.

n: The king calls Daniel “master of the magicians,” his official title, and trusts that no mystery is too hard for him.

f.w: master of the magicians

n: In his dream he saw an enormous tree in the center of the earth.

f.w: a tree in the midst of the earth

n: The tree grows until it reaches the sky and can be seen from the ends of the earth—like the tower of Babel, a symbol of human ambition reaching toward heaven.

f.w: the height thereof reached unto heaven

n: Its leaves are beautiful and its fruit abundant, feeding and sheltering every creature. A great empire could provide protection and prosperity for many peoples.

f.w: the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof

n: A “watcher,” a holy one, comes down from heaven. This is an angelic messenger who watches over the earth on God’s behalf.

f.w: a watcher and an holy one

n: The angel commands that the tree be cut down, its branches lopped, its leaves shaken off, and its fruit scattered. All who relied on it flee.

f.w: Hew down

n: But the stump and roots remain, bound with iron and bronze. Partway through, the imagery shifts from a tree to a person living among animals, soaked with dew.

f.w: leave the stump of his roots in the earth
f.g: A sign of hope: the tree can grow back.

n: His mind will become like an animal’s for “seven times”—probably seven years, or a complete period of time.

f.w: seven times
f.g: Likely seven years; seven also suggests a full, complete period.

n: The purpose is clear: so that everyone may know that the Most High rules over human kingdoms and gives them to whomever He chooses—even the lowliest of people.

f.w: the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men
the basest of men

n: The king ends his account and asks Daniel to interpret, since only he can.
Daniel is stunned and troubled—he cares about the king and dreads delivering bad news. The king reassures him. Daniel wishes the dream applied to the king’s enemies instead.

f.w: astonied for one hour
f.g: Stunned for a while (“hour” = a short time).

n: Daniel begins by restating the dream’s image of the great tree.
He repeats its beauty and how it fed and sheltered all creatures.
“It is thou, O king.” Like Nathan telling David “Thou art the man,” Daniel boldly names the king as the tree.

f.w: It is thou, O king

n: Daniel recounts the angel’s command to cut down the tree but leave its stump.
This is the decree of the Most High, not merely a dream.

The king will be driven from human society, live like an animal, and eat grass like cattle until he acknowledges that God rules. Some historians link this to a rare mental illness in which a person behaves like an animal.

f.w: till thou know that the most High ruleth

n: The stump means his kingdom will be restored once he learns that heaven rules. Judgment is meant to teach, not just to punish.

f.w: the heavens do rule
f.g: “Heaven” used as a respectful way of referring to God.

n: Daniel lovingly urges repentance: stop sinning, do what is right, and show mercy to the poor. Perhaps God will delay the judgment. Repentance always opens a door.

f.w: break off thy sins by righteousness
shewing mercy to the poor

n: Everything happens just as foretold. The narration now shifts to the third person.
A year passes. God gave the king time to repent.
Walking on his palace roof, Nebuchadnezzar boasts: “Is this not great Babylon, which I built by my power for my glory?” Ancient inscriptions show he did boast of his building projects in Babylon.

f.w: Is not this great Babylon

n: Even as he speaks, a voice from heaven declares that his kingdom is taken from him. Pride is answered immediately.

f.w: While the word was in the king's mouth

n: The voice repeats the sentence: he will live like an animal until he learns who truly rules.
It happens at once. He lives outdoors like an ox, his hair grows like feathers and his nails like claws. The proud king is reduced to the level of an animal.

f.w: did eat grass as oxen

n: Back to first person: at the end of the period, the king looks up to heaven—and his sanity returns. Looking up to God is the turning point. He praises the eternal God.

f.w: lifted up mine eyes unto heaven
his kingdom is from generation to generation

n: All earth’s inhabitants are as nothing compared to God, who does as He wills in heaven and earth. No one can stop Him or demand an explanation.

f.w: none can stay his hand
the army of heaven

n: His reason, honor, and kingdom are restored—with even greater majesty. God restores the humble.

f.w: excellent majesty was added unto me

n: The king’s final testimony: he praises the King of heaven, whose works are true and whose ways are just—and who can humble the proud. Nebuchadnezzar learned this lesson the hard way.

f.w: those that walk in pride he is able to abase
abase
